question_text: The conventional approach to understanding political attitudes arranges which terms along a continuum?
option_a: Capitalist, socialist, communist and fascist
option_b: Traditional, charismatic, legal-rational and populist
option_c: Parochial, subject, participant and civic
option_d: Radical, liberal, moderate, conservative and reactionary
explanation: The source states that the conventional approach is to arrange the terms radical, liberal, moderate, conservative and reactionary along a continuum in order to gain a perspective or understanding of each of them.

question_text: According to the source, which four things are relevant to the understanding of political change?
option_a: Cost, benefit, risk and reward
option_b: Direction, depth, speed and method
option_c: Ideology, party, leadership and finance
option_d: Participation, transparency, accountability and legitimacy
explanation: The source identifies four things relevant to the understanding of political change: the direction the proposed change will carry society, the depth of the proposed change, the speed at which people want change, and the method by which it occurs.

question_text: In assessing the 'depth' of a proposed political change, what question is being asked?
option_a: Whether the change is progressive or retrogressive
option_b: Whether the desired change amounts to a major or minor adjustment, and whether it would modify or replace an institution fundamental to society
option_c: Whether the change will occur peacefully or violently
option_d: Whether the change enjoys the support of the majority
explanation: The source explains that the second criterion is to determine the depth of a proposed change -- whether the desired change would amount to a major or minor adjustment in society, and whether it would modify or replace an institution that is fundamental to the society as it now exists.

question_text: What relationship does the source draw between dissatisfaction and the speed of desired change?
option_a: Dissatisfaction has no effect on the speed at which change is demanded
option_b: The more dissatisfied people are with the status quo, the more slowly they want change
option_c: Only the educated demand rapid change
option_d: The more dissatisfied the people are with the status quo, the more impatient they are likely to be, and therefore the more rapidly they want change
explanation: The source states that the third aspect is the speed at which people want change, and that the more dissatisfied the people are with the status quo, the more impatient they are likely to be and therefore the more rapidly they want to change.

question_text: Which examples does the source give of political change achieved illegally?
option_a: Russia in 1917 and China in 1949
option_b: Britain in 1215 and America in 1776
option_c: Ghana in 1957 and Nigeria in 1960
option_d: Iran in 1979 and Afghanistan in 1982
explanation: The source states that the last factor is the method by which change occurs -- peacefully or violently, legally or extra-legally -- and that political change can be achieved illegally as it was attained in Russia in 1917 or China in 1949.

question_text: Where on the political spectrum is the radical located, and what change does the radical favour?
option_a: On the right, favouring a return to former values
option_b: In the centre, favouring gradual adjustment
option_c: On the extreme right, favouring superficial alterations only
option_d: On the extreme left, favouring an immediate and fundamental -- that is, revolutionary -- change in society
explanation: The source states that a radical is on the extreme left of the spectrum of political attitude, can be impatient with less than extreme proposals, and that all radicals favour an immediate and fundamental change in the society -- in other words, all radicals favour revolutionary change.

question_text: How does the source describe the liberal's position on the continuum?
option_a: Furthest from the status quo point, and wholly opposed to existing society
option_b: Identical to the conservative position in every respect
option_c: Close to the status quo point, significantly less dissatisfied than the radicals, supporting the basic features of society while anxious to reform its weaknesses
option_d: Committed to returning society to a previous condition
explanation: The source states that liberals are close to the status quo point on the continuum, which makes them significantly less dissatisfied with the existing state of affairs than the radicals; they support the basic features of society but are quick to recognize weakness and are anxious to reform the system.

question_text: What does the source identify as one of the most fundamental differences between a radical and a liberal?
option_a: Their attitude towards foreign policy
option_b: Their attitude towards the law
option_c: Their views on the role of religion in society
option_d: Their preferred method of taxation
explanation: The source states that one of the most fundamental differences between a radical and a liberal is the attitude of each toward the law: radicals, being opposed to the political system that governs them, often see the law as one way in which those who dominate society maintain their control, while liberals generally respect the concept of law.

question_text: Moderates are characterised in the source by which position?
option_a: They reject all change of any kind
option_b: They are fundamentally satisfied with society, but insist that changes be made gradually and that no change be so extreme as to disrupt the society
option_c: They favour revolutionary change carried out peacefully
option_d: They seek to return society to a former value system
explanation: The source states that moderates are fundamentally satisfied with the society, although they agree there is room for improvement and recognize specific areas needing modification, but insist that changes should be made gradually and that no change should be so extreme as to disrupt the society.

question_text: Why do conservatives support the status quo, according to the source?
option_a: Because they are legally obliged to do so
option_b: Because they have never considered any alternative
option_c: Because they wish to return to a previous condition of society
option_d: Not so much because they like it, but because they believe it is the best that can be achieved now
explanation: The source states that conservatives support the status quo not so much because they like it, but because they believe that it is the best that can be achieved now, lacking confidence in society's ability to achieve improvements through bold policy initiatives.

question_text: Which point on the political spectrum alone proposes retrogressive change?
option_a: The radical
option_b: The liberal
option_c: The conservative
option_d: The reactionary
explanation: The source states that of all the political attitudes, only the reactionaries propose retrogressive changes -- that is, a policy that would return society to a previous condition or even a former value system.

question_text: Which historical example does the source use to illustrate reactionary change?
option_a: The Russian Revolution of 1917 under Lenin
option_b: The Chinese Revolution of 1949 under Mao
option_c: The overthrow of the Shah of Iran in 1979, after which the government headed by Ayatollah Khomeini returned the country to the pre-Shah era
option_d: The Cuban Revolution of 1959 under Castro
explanation: The source gives as an example of reactionary change that when the Shah of Iran was overthrown in 1979, the new government headed by Ayatollah Khomeini returned the country to the pre-Shah era.

question_text: On the question of rights, how do left-wing and right-wing attitudes differ?
option_a: Both place identical emphasis on property rights
option_b: The left considers property rights inalienable while the right rejects them
option_c: Neither is concerned with rights of any kind
option_d: The left emphasises the extension of human rights, while the right emphasises economic or property rights and considers property right an inalienable right
explanation: The source states that the left is inclined towards personal liberty especially as conceived in human rights, placing emphasis on the extension of human rights, while rightist-minded political attitudes put emphasis on economic or property rights, indeed considering property right as an inalienable right.

question_text: On the question of rationalism, what position does the source attribute to the right?
option_a: The right believes wholly in human rationality and the scientific method
option_b: The right holds that human beings can always improve upon existing conditions
option_c: The right rejects all established institutions as irrational
option_d: Right-wing attitudes tend toward irrationalism, believing in the known, tried and tested methods and institutions of society
explanation: The source states that right-wing political attitudes tend toward irrationalism -- for example, conservatives believe in the known, tried and tested methods and institutions of society and do not usually accept that human beings can make improvement upon existing conditions -- while the left believes in human rationality.

question_text: How does the source characterise leftist thinking on national frontiers?
option_a: Leftists believe in internationalism, insisting national frontiers are artificial and meant to promote exploitation, the boundary they recognize being human and not geographical
option_b: Leftists regard national sovereignty as sacred and inviolable
option_c: Leftists believe frontiers should be redrawn along ethnic lines
option_d: Leftists accept nationalism and metaphysical thinking
explanation: The source states that rightists believe in nationalism and metaphysical thinking, while leftists believe in internationalism, insisting that national frontiers are artificial and meant to promote exploitation in the name of national sovereignty and non-interference in domestic affairs -- the boundary leftists recognize being human and not geographical.

question_text: On the question of equality, the source states which contrast?
option_a: The left is elitist whilst the right is equalitarian minded
option_b: Both left and right reject the idea of equality
option_c: Both left and right hold identical views on equality
option_d: The left is equalitarian minded whilst the right is elitist
explanation: The source states that the left is equalitarian minded whilst the right is elitist; leftists emphasize the basic equality of humanity, while rightists argue that society is stratified and that human beings are unevenly endowed, some being innately superior to others.

question_text: According to the leftist argument in the source, what is the consequence when an individual's talent is not developed?
option_a: The individual alone bears the loss
option_b: The talent will develop naturally in the next generation
option_c: The state must compensate the individual financially
option_d: It is not the individual that suffers from it, but the society as a whole
explanation: The source records the leftist argument that men have equal talent or latent ability, that once all talents have been developed each must be given equal opportunities to contribute to social development, and that if an individual's talent is not developed it is not the individual that suffers from it but the society as a whole.

question_text: What does the source identify as the primary motivating factor that many people suspect determines a citizen's political position?
option_a: Religious affiliation
option_b: Regional origin
option_c: Party membership
option_d: Economic pressures
explanation: The source states that many people suspect that economic pressures are the primary motivating factors that determine the particular political position a citizen takes, with other factors including age, educational status, psychological disposition and sex.

question_text: Why, according to the source, do elderly people tend to bother less about change than the youth?
option_a: Because they are generally better educated
option_b: Because they have very limited time to live, and so may not live long enough to enjoy the impact of the change
option_c: Because they hold most positions of political power
option_d: Because they are legally barred from participating in change
explanation: The source states that elderly people, unlike the youths, have very limited time to live, which makes them bother less about change, the impact of which they may not live long to enjoy, whereas the youths view issues of change as affecting their future.

question_text: How does the source describe the role of youths and the old in political change?
option_a: The old are the fuel for change and the youths resist it
option_b: Neither group has any significant role in political change
option_c: The youths are the fuel and raw materials for change, and the old people the major force that resists it
option_d: Both groups resist change equally
explanation: The source states that the age structure of a country's population is an important factor in political change, making the youths the fuel and raw materials for change and the old people the major force that resists it.

question_text: What effect does the source attribute to a lack of education on attitudes to political change?
option_a: The uneducated are always opposed to any change
option_b: The uneducated are indifferent to political change altogether
option_c: The uneducated do not possess the advantage of thoroughly weighing the merits and demerits of change, which makes the probability that they plunge society into change higher
option_d: Education has no measurable effect on attitudes to change
explanation: The source states that the uneducated do not possess the advantage of thoroughly weighing the merits and demerits of change, a factor that makes the probability that they plunge the society into change higher, whereas the educated can properly evaluate the content and impact of a proposed change.

question_text: Why does the source say the attitude of the property class to change is generally protective?
option_a: Because they are prohibited by law from supporting change
option_b: Because in most societies the bulk of the property class is educated, so their attitude to change will be influenced by the desire to preserve their interests
option_c: Because they lack the education to evaluate proposals
option_d: Because they are usually the youngest section of the population
explanation: The source states that in most societies, since the bulk of the property class is educated, their attitude to change will certainly be influenced by the desire to preserve such interests.

question_text: According to the source, what made ideologies necessary?
option_a: The rise of the nation-state after the Treaty of Westphalia
option_b: The challenges of the Age of Enlightenment, when people believed they could improve their conditions by taking positive action instead of passively accepting life as it came
option_c: The collapse of the Soviet Union in 1991
option_d: The founding of the United Nations after the Second World War
explanation: The source states that ideologies were made necessary due to the challenges of the Age of Enlightenment, when people believed they could improve their conditions by taking positive action instead of passively accepting life as it came, a view reinforced by the democratization of politics and the upheavals of the Industrial Revolution.

question_text: Frederick Watkins suggested that ideology comes almost entirely from where, and with what characteristics?
option_a: From the political centre; always supportive of gradual reform
option_b: From the political extremes; always opposed to the status quo, proposing abrupt change, and usually militant, revolutionary and violent
option_c: From academic institutions; always theoretical and detached from practice
option_d: From religious bodies; always concerned with moral rather than political questions
explanation: The source states that Frederick Watkins suggests ideology comes almost entirely from the political extremes, is always opposed to the status quo, proposes an abrupt change in the existing order, and is usually militant, revolutionary and violent, as well as simplistic and utopian.

question_text: Which two documents does the source cite as falling within Watkins's definition of ideology?
option_a: The Magna Carta and the Bill of Rights
option_b: The Wealth of Nations and Das Capital
option_c: The American Declaration of Independence and the Communist Manifesto
option_d: The Articles of Confederation and the US Constitution
explanation: The source cites the American Declaration of Independence, a political statement authored by Thomas Jefferson, and the Communist Manifesto, an economic doctrine written by Karl Marx and Engels, as examples falling within Watkins's definition.

question_text: What did Karl Marx argue an ideology is?
option_a: A value system that provides a picture of the world as it is and as it should be
option_b: Nothing more than a fabrication used by the ruling class to justify their rule over the masses
option_c: An assessment of the status quo combined with a view of the future
option_d: The scientific method applied to the study of society
explanation: The source states that Karl Marx argues ideology is nothing more than a fabrication used by the ruling class to justify their rule over the masses, so that the dominant political ideas of any society always reflect the interests of the ruling classes.

question_text: Despite differing emphases, what do the various definitions of ideology have in common according to the source?
option_a: That ideology is primarily a political term, and consists of a view of the present and a vision of the future
option_b: That ideology is primarily an economic term concerned only with production
option_c: That ideology must always be violent in its methods
option_d: That ideology is confined to the twentieth century
explanation: The source concludes that although the definitions differ in emphasis, they have enough in common: ideology is primarily a political term, though applicable to other contexts, and it consists of a view of the present and a vision of the future.

question_text: The rudiments of capitalism were developed from which notion, in which book?
option_a: Adam Smith's notion of the 'invisible hands' in The Wealth of Nations
option_b: Karl Marx's notion of surplus value in Das Capital
option_c: John Locke's notion of natural rights in the Two Treatises
option_d: Jean Bodin's notion of sovereignty in Science Politique
explanation: The source states that the rudiments of capitalism were developed from Adam Smith's notion of the 'invisible hands' in his book The Wealth of Nations (1776).

question_text: The principle of Laissez-Faire advocated by Adam Smith holds which of the following?
option_a: That government should remain aloof of economic matters and allow the forces of demand and supply to direct the economy, thereby encouraging competition
option_b: That government should own all major industries
option_c: That government should fix all prices and wages
option_d: That government should nationalise the banks and heavy industries
explanation: The source states that Smith advocated the principle of Laissez-Faire, which held that government should remain aloof of economic matters but should rather allow the forces of demand and supply to direct the economy, thereby encouraging competition.

question_text: Why is competition regarded as the engine of the capitalist system?
option_a: Because it guarantees equality of outcome for all citizens
option_b: Because it rests on the assumption that the good of the whole is best served when each person pursues his or her own self interest
option_c: Because it eliminates the need for private property
option_d: Because it allows the state to plan the economy efficiently
explanation: The source states that competition is regarded as the engine of the capitalist system because it rested on the assumption that the good of the whole is best served when each person pursues his or her own self interest.

question_text: Capitalism is defined in the source as an economic system under which which of the following is true?
option_a: The means of production are publicly owned and centrally planned
option_b: All citizens own an equal share of the means of production
option_c: The ownership of the means of production is concentrated in the hands of a minor section of the society
option_d: The means of production are owned collectively by workers' cooperatives
explanation: The source defines capitalism as an economic system under which the ownership of the means of production is concentrated in the hands of a minor section of the society.

question_text: According to Awolowo (1978), capitalism has which four basic concepts?
option_a: Competition, profit, accumulation and expansion
option_b: Public ownership, welfare, planning and socialist intent
option_c: Private property, choice, equality and egoistic altruism
option_d: Liberty, equality, fraternity and justice
explanation: The source states that according to Awolowo capitalism has four basic concepts: private property, choice, equality and egoistic altruism.

question_text: What does 'egoistic altruism', which Smith called the 'invisible hands', suggest?
option_a: That individuals should deliberately sacrifice their interests for others
option_b: That the state must intervene to reconcile competing interests
option_c: That while pursuing his own economic interest, every individual unconsciously promotes at the same time the economic interest of others
option_d: That economic self-interest always harms the wider society
explanation: The source explains that egoistic-altruism, or what Smith called the 'invisible hands', suggests that while pursuing his economic interest every individual unconsciously promotes at the same time the economic interest of others.

question_text: Historically, when did capitalism develop, and what was its springboard?
option_a: After the French Revolution, with the Declaration of the Rights of Man as its springboard
option_b: After the collapse of the feudal system, with the Industrial Revolution in 18th century England as its springboard
option_c: After the Treaty of Westphalia, with the rise of the sovereign state as its springboard
option_d: After the Second World War, with the Marshall Plan as its springboard
explanation: The source states that historically capitalism developed after the collapse of the feudal system, its springboard being the Industrial Revolution in 18th century England, where mechanization replaced human labour and led to mass production of goods and services.

question_text: Why is capitalism said in the source to be related to democracy?
option_a: Because both require a written constitution to operate
option_b: Because both were invented in the United States
option_c: Because both reject the idea of private property
option_d: Because both emphasize freedom of choice and individualism, otherwise referred to as the survival of the fittest
explanation: The source states that capitalism is related to democracy since both emphasize freedom of choice and individualism, otherwise referred to as the survival of the fittest, and that although capitalism originated in Europe, the United States is today regarded as the bastion of capitalism in the world.

question_text: According to Marx and Engels, socialism occupies which position?
option_a: The final stage of human historical development
option_b: A stage preceding feudalism
option_c: An intermediate stage between capitalism and communism
option_d: An alternative to communism that rejects class analysis
explanation: The source states that according to Karl Marx and Fredrick Engels, socialism is an intermediate stage between capitalism and communism.

question_text: Which three basic features does socialism have, according to the source?
option_a: Public ownership of the means of production, distribution and finance; the establishment of a welfare state; and socialist intent
option_b: Private property, choice and competition
option_c: Nationalisation, militarisation and one-party rule
option_d: Planning, taxation and redistribution
explanation: The source states that socialism has three basic features: public ownership of the means of production, distribution and finance; the establishment of a welfare state; and a socialist intent.

question_text: What is described in the source as central to socialism, and what is the traditional way of socializing an economy?
option_a: Competition is central, and the traditional method is deregulation
option_b: Taxation is central, and the traditional method is redistribution
option_c: Welfare is central, and the traditional method is direct cash transfer
option_d: Planning is central, and the traditional way is by nationalization
explanation: The source states that in order to achieve socialism's goals planning is central to it, and that the traditional way to socialize an economy is by nationalization -- though socialists are wary of this measure because of the problems associated with it.

question_text: What does the principle of socialist intent set as its goal, and what replaces competition under socialism?
option_a: Maximising national output, with state monopoly replacing competition
option_b: Achieving military strength, with discipline replacing competition
option_c: Making citizens free from material dependence, with co-operation expected to replace competition
option_d: Guaranteeing property rights, with regulation replacing competition
explanation: The source states that the principle of socialist intent sets the goal of making citizens free from material dependence, and that since scarcity under capitalism makes people compete acutely, under socialism co-operation is expected to replace competition.

question_text: How does the source describe the relationship between socialism and democracy?
option_a: Socialism is fundamentally incompatible with democracy
option_b: Democracy is a stage that must be abolished before socialism can begin
option_c: Socialism is the economic equivalent of democracy -- it is to the individual economically what democracy is to the individual politically
option_d: Socialism and democracy are identical in every respect
explanation: The source states that in some respects socialism is compatible with democracy, since it is to the individual economically what democracy is to the individual politically, and that socialism is therefore the economic equivalent of democracy.

question_text: Utopian socialism, associated with Saint Simon and Robert Owen, differs from the Marxian approach in which respect?
option_a: It sought to achieve socialist ends through peaceful means
option_b: It rejected public ownership of the means of production
option_c: It insisted on the dictatorship of the proletariat
option_d: It denied that class differences exist
explanation: The source states that the Utopian socialism of Saint Simon and Robert Owen is different from the Marxian approach because it sought to achieve socialist ends through peaceful means, while scientific socialism strictly followed the doctrinaire exposition of Marx and Engels.

question_text: Which African leaders are associated in the source with Ujamaa and Humanism respectively?
option_a: President Nyerere of Tanzania and President Kaunda of Zambia
option_b: Kwame Nkrumah of Ghana and Gamal Abdul Nasser of Egypt
option_c: Obafemi Awolowo of Nigeria and Nnamdi Azikiwe of Nigeria
option_d: Mengistu Haile Mariam of Ethiopia and Samora Machel of Mozambique
explanation: The source states that in the early days of African independence some African leaders, notably President Nyerere of Tanzania and President Kaunda of Zambia, toyed with the idea of African socialism, which they called Ujamaa and Humanism respectively, while in Nigeria Chief Awolowo advocated Democratic Socialism.

question_text: Which saying does the source cite to illustrate the lack of unanimity about socialism as an ideology?
option_a: All socialists are Marxists, but not all Marxists are socialists
option_b: Not all socialists are Marxists, but all Marxists are socialists
option_c: Socialism is the economic equivalent of democracy
option_d: He who says organization says oligarchy
explanation: The source states that because of the lack of unanimity of view about socialism as an ideology, it is not unusual to hear people say: not all socialists are Marxists, but all Marxists are socialists.

question_text: Communism is based on the doctrine developed by Marx and Engels in which book, written in which year?
option_a: Das Capital, written in 1867
option_b: The State and Revolution, written in 1917
option_c: The Wealth of Nations, written in 1776
option_d: The Communist Manifesto, written in 1848
explanation: The source states that communism is a social and political system based on the doctrine developed by Karl Marx and Fredrick Engels in their book The Communist Manifesto, written in 1848.

question_text: According to communist doctrine as presented in the source, what is the relationship between the economy and other spheres of society?
option_a: Politics determines the economy, which is part of the superstructure
option_b: The economy and politics are wholly independent of each other
option_c: The economy is the foundation of societies, while politics, religion and others -- called the superstructure -- are determined by the economic factor
option_d: Religion determines both politics and the economy
explanation: The source states that communism teaches that the economy is the foundation of societies, while others such as politics and religion, which they called the superstructure, are determined by the economic factor.

question_text: What does communist theory hold will be installed as a first step after the proletariat emerges victorious?
option_a: A parliamentary democracy with universal suffrage
option_b: A dictatorship of the proletariat, to eliminate all differences before the state apparatus disappears
option_c: A federal constitution with checks and balances
option_d: A coalition government of workers and the bourgeoisie
explanation: The source states that as a first step a dictatorship of the proletariat will be installed to eliminate all differences before the state apparatus will disappear.

question_text: What is identified in the source as a major feature of communism?
option_a: Regular competitive elections between rival parties
option_b: The complete absence of any bureaucracy
option_c: The dominance of a one party organization
option_d: The protection of private enterprise in key sectors
explanation: The source states that a major feature of communism is the dominance of a one party organization, noting that in the Soviet Union arguments could only be made about the interpretation of Marxism-Leninism, not about alternatives to it, and that communism also demands a strong bureaucracy and considerable curtailment of freedom.

question_text: Who introduced the ideas of 'Glasnost' and 'Perestroika', and in what year did he emerge?
option_a: V. I. Lenin, in 1917
option_b: Joseph Stalin, in 1924
option_c: Mikhail Gorbachev, in 1985
option_d: Georgie Plekhanov, in 1898
explanation: The source states that communism demanded a considerable curtailment of freedom until the emergence of Mikhail Gorbachev in 1985, who introduced the ideas of 'Glasnost' and 'Perestroika' to reform the practice of communism in the old Soviet Union, which ultimately led to the collapse of the Soviet-communist state and the abandonment of the ideology.

question_text: How does the source distinguish a revolution from an evolution?
option_a: A revolution is always peaceful while an evolution is always violent
option_b: A revolution is a sudden or abrupt change in the social structure, while evolution is a gradual, stage-by-stage progression from one level to another
option_c: A revolution affects only the government while an evolution affects the whole society
option_d: There is no meaningful distinction between the two
explanation: The source defines a revolution as a sudden or abrupt change in the social structure of a society, distinct from evolution, which is a gradual stage-by-stage progression, transition or development from one level to another -- revolution being an unusual and often unorthodox means of effecting change.

question_text: Following Nisbet, how is a revolution described in the source?
option_a: As an economic process driven purely by market forces
option_b: As a spontaneous outburst that cannot be planned
option_c: As a purely military operation with no social objectives
option_d: As political in character, concerned with the calculated overthrow of an existing political order, using as much force and terror as deemed necessary to effect radical changes in men's moral, economic, social and intellectual lives
explanation: The source cites Nisbet in conceiving a revolution as political in character: concerned with the calculated overthrow of an existing political order, using as much force and terror as are deemed necessary to effect radical changes in men's moral, economic, social and intellectual lives.

question_text: Besides political character, what two other prerequisites does the source say a revolution requires to succeed?
option_a: Religious zeal or mentality, in addition to military tactics
option_b: Foreign funding and international recognition
option_c: A written constitution and an elected assembly
option_d: Trade union backing and press freedom
explanation: The source states that for a revolution to succeed it also requires two other prerequisites: religious zeal or mentality, in addition to military tactics -- noting that without the religious, almost messianic preoccupation, the Jacobins would not have succeeded in carrying out the French Revolution.

question_text: Which conditions does the source identify as making violent change inevitable?
option_a: Poverty, political deprivation or exclusion, and social injustice
option_b: Rapid industrialisation and urban growth
option_c: The existence of multiple political parties
option_d: High literacy rates and press freedom
explanation: The source states that a revolution never occurs unless the objective conditions are ripe, which makes violent change inevitable, and that these conditions include poverty, political deprivation or exclusion and social injustice, with lack of access to basic human needs being prime causes.

question_text: Which statement by former President John Kennedy is cited in the source on the conditions contributing to revolution?
option_a: Ask not what your country can do for you
option_b: Political power flows from the barrel of the gun
option_c: Those who make peaceful change impossible make violent change inevitable
option_d: The peace of the grave yard is no peace at all
explanation: The source quotes former President John Kennedy explaining one condition that contributes to a revolution: those who make peaceful change impossible make violent change inevitable.

question_text: Contrary to popular impression, what does the source say about the spontaneity of revolutions?
option_a: A revolution is not necessarily spontaneous; it has to be planned and led for it to be meaningful and enduring
option_b: Revolutions are always entirely spontaneous
option_c: Only failed revolutions are planned
option_d: Spontaneity is the single most important ingredient of revolution
explanation: The source states that contrary to popular impression, a revolution is not necessarily spontaneous; it has to be planned and be led for it to be meaningful and enduring.

question_text: Which group led by Georgie Plekhanov, the father of Russian Marxism, insisted that Russia was not ripe for revolution because it was still a feudal society?
option_a: The Bolsheviks
option_b: The Jacobins
option_c: The Nationalists
option_d: The Mensheviks
explanation: The source states that the Mensheviks, led by the father of Russian Marxism Georgie Plekhanov, were the orthodox Marxists who insisted the dialectics had to run its full course before the proletarian revolution, and that Russia was not ripe for revolution because it was still a feudal society in the pre-1917 years.

question_text: On what ground did the Bolsheviks, led by Lenin, reject the Menshevik position?
option_a: They rejected it as too dogmatic, arguing that under certain circumstances the proletariat and the peasantries could join forces and take control of the state
option_b: They argued that Russia had already passed through the capitalist stage
option_c: They insisted that revolution should be achieved only through peaceful means
option_d: They held that no revolution was possible in Russia at all
explanation: The source states that the Bolsheviks led by V. I. Lenin rejected the Menshevik theory as too dogmatic, arguing that under certain circumstances the proletariat and the peasantries could join forces and take control of the state.

question_text: How did Lenin modify Marxist theory, according to the source?
option_a: He removed violence from the doctrine and confined it to advanced states
option_b: He restored violence to the doctrine, amended the theory to apply to underdeveloped states, and filled in the blank space Marx had left regarding post-revolution proletarian society
option_c: He rejected the idea of a proletarian revolution entirely
option_d: He argued that revolution would occur automatically without leadership
explanation: The source states that Lenin restored violence to the doctrine, amended the theory to make it apply to underdeveloped states, and filled in the blank space that Marx had left regarding post-revolution proletarian society.

question_text: What did Lenin believe about the proletariat and class-consciousness?
option_a: That the proletariat would develop class-consciousness naturally over time
option_b: That labour unions were the ideal body to ignite the revolution
option_c: That class-consciousness was irrelevant to revolution
option_d: That the proletariat would not develop class-consciousness without the intervention of a revolutionary group, since someone must ignite the revolution
explanation: The source states that Lenin believed the proletariat would not develop class-consciousness without the intervention of a revolutionary group, that someone must ignite the revolution, and that he did not recommend even the labour unions because they could be bought over.

question_text: What did Lenin mean by the 'revolutionary vanguard'?
option_a: The mass of the peasantry acting spontaneously
option_b: A small, disciplined, totally dedicated group by which a minority could impose socialism
option_c: An alliance of labour unions and student bodies
option_d: The elected representatives of the working class in parliament
explanation: The source states that Lenin believed socialism could be imposed by a minority -- a revolutionary vanguard, a small, disciplined, totally dedicated group requiring total commitment.

question_text: The Bolshevik party, which served as the vanguard of the proletariat in Russia, was renamed what, and in what year?
option_a: The Communist Party, in 1918
option_b: The Menshevik Party, in 1917
option_c: The Socialist Party, in 1924
option_d: The International Communist Movement, in 1921
explanation: The source states that the vanguard of the proletariat in Russia was the Bolshevik party, which was renamed the Communist Party in 1918.

question_text: In what month and year did Lenin's Bolshevik party carry out the socialist revolution in Russia, and when did Lenin die?
option_a: March 1917; he died in 1918
option_b: February 1918; he died in 1921
option_c: October 1917; he died in 1924
option_d: November 1919; he died in 1928
explanation: The source states that Lenin succeeded in October 1917 when the Bolshevik party carried out the socialist revolution in Russia, which eventually led to the formation of the USSR led first by Lenin himself, who later died in 1924.

question_text: In what year was the Communist Party of China founded?
explanation: The source states that the Communist Party of China was founded in the year 1921, and that Mao Tse-tung, the leader of the revolution, was born in 1893.

question_text: In his Report on the Hunan Peasant Movement, what did Mao call upon the Communists to do?
option_a: To ally with the Nationalists against foreign powers
option_b: To concentrate on organising the industrial working class in the cities
option_c: To abandon the cities for the countryside, because the peasants and not the proletariat were China's true revolutionaries
option_d: To seek support from the Soviet Union before acting
explanation: The source states that Mao wrote a book titled Report on the Hunan Peasant Movement, which called upon the Communists to abandon the cities for the countryside because the peasants, not the proletariat, were China's true revolutionaries -- with this document Mao led the formation of what became Maoist thought.

question_text: According to the source, how many people embarked on the Long March, over what distance, and how many survived?
option_a: About 35,000 embarked, covering 1,000 miles, and 100,000 survived
option_b: About 100,000 embarked, covering 6,000 miles, and only 35,000 survived
option_c: About 6,000 embarked, covering 100,000 miles, and only 1,000 survived
option_d: About 60,000 embarked, covering 3,500 miles, and only 10,000 survived
explanation: The source states that about 100,000 people embarked on the Long March, a journey which covered 6,000 miles, and only 35,000 survived, with a new base established in Shensi province where the March ended.

question_text: Which phrase did Mao use to signal that he would allow the people to criticize his government, unlike the Soviet method of suppressing dissent?
option_a: Political power flows from the barrel of the gun
option_b: Let a hundred flowers bloom, let a hundred schools contend
option_c: Surround the cities with the countryside
option_d: Red over expert
explanation: The source states that Mao allowed the people to criticize his government, unlike the Soviet method of suppressing dissent and imposing conformity, and to achieve this Mao used the phrase: 'let a hundred flowers bloom, let a hundred schools contend'.

question_text: Mao rejected Lenin's elitist reliance on the party to lead the revolution, invoking which slogan?
option_a: Workers of the world unite
option_b: Self-government now
option_c: Red over expert
option_d: Knowledge must be put to work
explanation: The source states that Mao rejected Lenin's elitist reliance on the party to lead the revolution, invoking the slogan 'red over expert' and calling for the mobilization of the masses, which he called the last line of defence of the revolution.

question_text: Mao identified which two inseparable objectives of a revolution?
option_a: Economic and cultural
option_b: Domestic and international
option_c: Ideological and religious
option_d: Military and political
explanation: The source states that Mao identified two objectives of a revolution, military and political, the two being inseparable, since as he put it 'political power also flows from the barrel of the gun'.

question_text: According to Mao, what is the first military goal of a guerrilla war, and what alone is essential to the guerrilla?
option_a: To capture the capital city; the essential thing is foreign support
option_b: To preserve oneself and destroy the enemy by destroying his fighting capabilities; the only thing essential to the guerrilla is the safe zone
option_c: To win international recognition; the essential thing is a formal army
option_d: To negotiate a settlement; the essential thing is a political party
explanation: The source states that according to Mao the first military goal of a guerrilla war is to preserve oneself and destroy the enemy, which can be done by destroying the fighting capabilities of the opponent, and that the only thing essential to the guerrilla is the safe zone.

question_text: Which dictator did Fidel Castro overthrow in Cuba, and in what month and year?
option_a: Fulgencio Batista, in January 1953
option_b: Fulgencio Batista, in December 1959
option_c: Emperor Haile Selassie, in 1974
option_d: King Farouk, in 1952
explanation: The source states that Cuba was under a dictator named Fulgencio Batista, and that Castro, having built a following among the peasantry to whom he promised land reforms and redistribution, embarked on guerrilla warfare which eventually toppled the government of Batista in December 1959.

question_text: In 1961, which administration sponsored the Bay of Pigs insurrection against Castro's government?
option_a: The John Kennedy administration
option_b: The Eisenhower administration
option_c: The Lyndon Johnson administration
option_d: The Franklin Roosevelt administration
explanation: The source states that since assuming office in 1959 the communist-inspired government of Fidel Castro faced consistent United States hostility, which reached its peak in 1961 when the John Kennedy administration sponsored the Bay of Pigs insurrection against Castro's government.

question_text: In which fields does the source say the 1959 Cuban revolution recorded modest achievements?
option_a: Heavy industry, mining and shipbuilding
option_b: Banking, insurance and tourism
option_c: Education, public health and racial equality, with substantial investment in agriculture especially sugar-cane production
option_d: Military technology and space research
explanation: The source states that though still a third world country, the 1959 revolution has recorded modest achievements for Cuba in the fields of education, public health and racial equality, including substantial investment in agriculture, especially sugar-cane production, its major foreign exchange earner.

question_text: During the cold war years, what was the typical third world revolutionary movement?
option_a: A communist insurgency based in the countryside
option_b: A liberal reform movement based in the universities
option_c: A religious movement based in the cities
option_d: A trade union movement based in the industrial sector
explanation: The source states that during the cold war years the typical third world revolutionary movement was a communist insurgency based in the countryside, organised by those who viewed their leaders as promoting US imperialism.

question_text: According to the source, what did many third world revolutions actually amount to, despite their ideological labels?
option_a: Genuine contests between global communism and capitalism
option_b: Purely religious conflicts with no political content
option_c: Movements entirely directed from Moscow and Washington
option_d: Local power struggles largely between rural ethnic groups, into which the great powers were drawn for selfish reasons
explanation: The source states that in reality many of these governments and revolutions had little to do with global communism, capitalism or imperialism -- they were indeed local power struggles largely between rural ethnic groups into which great powers, for selfish reasons, were drawn.

question_text: Which radical group is cited in the source as running schools and hospitals and controlling 12 seats in Lebanon's parliament as at 2001?
option_a: The FLN
option_b: The Patriotic Front
option_c: Hezbollah
option_d: The African National Congress
explanation: The source states that radical groups like Hezbollah run schools and hospitals and controlled 12 seats in Lebanon's parliament as at 2001, and that through such activities they gain legitimacy in the eyes of their people rather than being perceived as terrorist organizations.

question_text: In Revolutionary Pressures in Africa, what did Claude Ake identify as the most salient feature of the post-colonial African state?
option_a: Ethnic pluralism arising from artificial boundaries
option_b: Neo-colonial dependency, rooted in and perpetuated by global class struggle
option_c: Military dominance over civilian institutions
option_d: The absence of any indigenous ruling class
explanation: The source states that in Revolutionary Pressures in Africa Claude Ake identified neo-colonial dependency as the most salient feature of a post-colonial African state, a condition rooted in and perpetuated by global class struggle, concluding that the class war can only be brought to an end through socialist revolution.

question_text: The Egyptian Revolution was launched in which year, by whom, and against which ruler?
option_a: In 1952, by Gamal Abdul Nasser, who led the army to overthrow King Farouk
option_b: In 1956, by Anwar Sadat, against the British
option_c: In 1974, by Mengistu Haile Mariam, against Emperor Haile Selassie
option_d: In 1949, by Mao Tse-tung, against the Nationalists
explanation: The source states that the Egyptian Revolution was launched in 1952 by Gamal Abdul Nasser when he led the army to overthrow King Farouk, beginning under a revolutionary petty-bourgeois leadership that revolted against the incapacity and corruption of the old regime.

question_text: Which major asset was nationalised in Egypt in 1956 as part of widening the state sector?
option_a: The Aswan Dam
option_b: The Egyptian National Assembly
option_c: The Suez Canal
option_d: The Nile Delta farmlands
explanation: The source states that one of the objectives of the Egyptian revolution was to widen considerably the state sector, a factor that led to the nationalization of heavy industries and big banks including the Suez Canal in 1956, in pursuit of the goals of Arab-socialism.

question_text: In the Ghanaian struggle for independence, what was Kwame Nkrumah's slogan, as against that of Dr Joseph Danquah of the UGCC?
option_a: Nkrumah demanded 'Self-Government within the shortest possible time', while Danquah demanded 'Self-Government Now'
option_b: Both demanded immediate self-government on identical terms
option_c: Nkrumah demanded 'Self-Government Now', while Danquah's slogan was 'Self-Government within the shortest possible time'
option_d: Nkrumah demanded dominion status while Danquah demanded a republic
explanation: The source states that Kwame Nkrumah advocated independence for 'Self-Government Now' as opposed to Dr Joseph Danquah of the United Gold Coast Convention, whose slogan was 'Self-Government within the shortest possible time'.

question_text: Ghana's achievement under Nkrumah is described in the source as which of the following?
option_a: The first black African country to gain independence, in 1957
option_b: The first African country to adopt a socialist constitution
option_c: The first country to expel a colonial power by armed force
option_d: The first African country to hold multi-party elections
explanation: The source states that the militancy of Nkrumah's slogans, though it earned him detention where he won a colonial-supervised election, eventually succeeded in making Ghana the first black African country to gain independence in 1957.

question_text: Who led the 1974 Ethiopian Revolution, and which ruler was ousted?
option_a: Colonel Mengistu Haile Mariam, ousting Emperor Haile Selassie
option_b: Gamal Abdul Nasser, ousting King Farouk
option_c: Samora Machel, ousting the Portuguese administration
option_d: Laurent Kabila, ousting Mobutu Sese Seko
explanation: The source states that Colonel Mengistu Haile Mariam led the 1974 Ethiopian revolution, which ousted Emperor Haile Selassie from his authoritarian grip on power and exploitative feudal regime.

question_text: What is distinctive about the way the 1974 Ethiopian Revolution began?
option_a: It began as a peasant uprising in the countryside
option_b: It was initiated by students in the universities
option_c: It was organised from exile by an opposition party
option_d: It was initiated by the military, acting essentially in its own immediate interests, and later spread to the civilian population
explanation: The source states that it is important to note that the 1974 Ethiopian Revolution was initiated by the military, acting essentially in its own immediate interests, but this later spread to the civilian population in an outburst of general dissatisfaction.

question_text: In the Algerian liberation struggle, who provided the military vanguard and who supplied the intellectual sinew?
option_a: Robert Mugabe led the military effort while Joshua Nkomo supplied the intellectual sinew
option_b: The FLN led by Ahmed Ben Bella provided the military vanguard while Frantz Fanon supplied the intellectual sinew
option_c: Samora Machel provided the military vanguard while Sam Nujoma supplied the intellectual sinew
option_d: Nelson Mandela provided the military vanguard while Claude Ake supplied the intellectual sinew
explanation: The source states that in Algeria the FLN led by Ahmed Ben Bella provided the military vanguard while Frantz Fanon supplied the intellectual sinew.

question_text: In Zimbabwe, the Patriotic Front that led the liberation struggle was an amalgam of which two bodies, and who led it?
option_a: The ANC and PAC, led by Nelson Mandela
option_b: SWAPO and SWANU, led by Sam Nujoma
option_c: The FLN and FLNA, led by Ahmed Ben Bella
option_d: ZANU and ZAPU, led by Robert Mugabe and Joshua Nkomo
explanation: The source states that in Zimbabwe, Robert Mugabe and Joshua Nkomo of the Patriotic Front -- an amalgam of ZANU and ZAPU -- led the struggle.

question_text: Which countries does the source cite as examples where independence was negotiated rather than won through large-scale violence?
option_a: Nigeria, Sierra Leone and Gambia
option_b: Algeria, Zimbabwe and Namibia
option_c: Angola, Mozambique and Guinea-Bissau
option_d: Egypt, Ethiopia and Ghana
explanation: The source states that it was not all liberation struggles in Africa that entailed large scale violence -- there were countries such as Nigeria, Sierra Leone and Gambia where independence was negotiated.

question_text: In South Africa, majority rule was achieved in which year, following the unbanning of the ANC and the release of Nelson Mandela in which year?
option_a: Majority rule in 1994, following his release in 1990
option_b: Majority rule in 1990, following his release in 1985
option_c: Majority rule in 1996, following his release in 1994
option_d: Majority rule in 1992, following his release in 1989
explanation: The source states that in South Africa the African National Congress, after it was unbanned and its leader Nelson Mandela was released from prison in 1990, succeeded in achieving majority rule for the country in 1994.

question_text: The overthrow of Mobutu Sese Seko of former Zaire by Laurent Kabila is cited in the source as an example of what?
option_a: A guerrilla war aimed at independence from colonial rule
option_b: A reactionary movement returning society to a former value system
option_c: A negotiated transfer of power between political parties
option_d: An internal revolution against a despotic and authoritarian leader, in which a corrupt and unpopular leader was changed in a popular revolt
explanation: The source states that apart from guerrilla wars aimed at independence, African revolution also took internal forms like revolution against despotic and authoritarian leaders, citing the overthrow of Mobutu Sese Seko, the sit-tight ruler of former Zaire, by Laurent Kabila as another variant of a revolution, since a corrupt and unpopular leader was changed in a popular revolt.

question_text: Mahatma Gandhi's description of the situation in colonial India is quoted in the source in which phrase?
option_a: The peace of the grave yard
option_b: The last line of defence of the revolution
option_c: The interest of the stronger
option_d: Servitude in tranquility
explanation: The source cites Mahatma Gandhi's proverbial description of the situation in colonial India as 'the peace of the grave yard', used in questioning whether stability and peace are sustainable without social justice.
